editor_spans.body: The diplomacy over Ukraine is not only about Ukraine. In the Commons the Prime Minister presented the energy ceasefire as the quickest way to get diesel back onto world markets.

The government's own response to the US-Russia agreement also points to the effect on energy prices and the cost of living. The Chancellor speaks of conflicts in the Middle East and Europe 'hitting people across the world'.

This is the long-term thread behind this month's statements. A British government whose domestic standing rests on household bills now has a direct material stake in whether Russia stops striking refineries and grids. Its leverage over that question runs mainly through Washington, which brokered the ceasefire, rather than through London.

Set against the language of 'rock-solid' support 'for as long as it takes', the newly accelerated sums are small. Only £10 million of a £45 million missile package is being brought forward for winter. The larger £1.6 billion LMM commitment was already spread over four years.

Much of the rest consists of instructions to ministers to 'draw up' packages and appeals to partners to follow Britain's LNG ban. Britain's real role is convenor and exhorter, constrained by its fiscal room, while the decisive levers on supply and ceasefire sit elsewhere.

Three announcements in one week share a single idea of government: moving the centre of gravity out of London. GBR's headquarters goes to Derby, 'No10 North' is invoked in Scotland, and Burnham presses Holyrood to push power down to regions and cities. It is the politics of a former metro mayor now running the state.

The Scottish offer is the more combustible part. A Westminster Prime Minister is describing the Scottish Government as one of Europe's most centralised administrations. He is proposing to work with Scottish regions through the Scotland Office.

However warmly framed, that creates a channel for UK government to deal with Scottish places directly, around Holyrood. After 27 years of devolution built on the premise that Edinburgh speaks for Scotland, that is a structural challenge, not merely a policy offer.
The Derby move should be judged by scale as well as symbolism. The headquarters will hold up to 450 staff, and 600 apprenticeships are spread over four years.
Meanwhile less than 7% of the rail workforce is under 25, which means a retirement wave is coming that a few hundred apprentices a year will not by themselves replace.

The early 'benefits' of public ownership, such as frozen fares and extra seats, are real. But they are choices funded by the Treasury, and they will be tested when the bill for renewal and the ageing workforce comes due.

The most consequential line of the Commons statement is not about the 20 November summit itself. It is the Prime Minister's opening of a 'serious dialogue' on the long-term UK-EU relationship, with the public as 'the boss'. That is the first open signal from a governing party that the Brexit settlement itself is back on the table.

The case is being built from the bottom up, through the cost of the current settlement to exporters. Examples include document checks on salmon, banned seed potatoes and shellfish, and £1,400 burdens on single shipments.

Framing a decade as 'drift and division', and insisting that sticking with the status quo is a 'dereliction of duty', prepares the ground politically. Even so, the government is keeping its promised gains modest: £10 billion a year, and only by 2040.
